summary_text:
On January 8, 2024, the patient's left arm was entrapped in industrial machinery, sustaining a crush injury so severe that factory responders applied a tourniquet on scene and emergency crews had to dismantle the machine to free him. He arrived with a cold, pulseless hand, exposed bone, and a GCS of 11 with a reported brief loss of consciousness. Paramedics established IV access and gave fentanyl 100mcg before transferring him to the Midwest Regional trauma unit, where Dr. David Cho documented complete traumatic amputation at the level between the shoulder and elbow, with complete transection of the brachial artery and nerves, massive soft tissue loss, and traumatic shock from blood loss. X-ray and CT angiography confirmed a comminuted, displaced supracondylar humerus fracture with open segmental forearm and hand fractures, carpal disarray, and complete vascular disruption — an unsalvageable limb. He received two units of packed red blood cells and was taken emergently to the operating room the same day.

Dr. David Cho performed a left transhumeral amputation, sectioning the humerus at the junction of the middle and distal thirds, ligating and dividing the brachial artery, and performing traction neurectomy of the median, ulnar, and radial nerves with bupivacaine 0.5% injection before myofascial closure. He recovered in the ICU, was transitioned from IV PCA Dilaudid to oral oxycodone and gabapentin 300mg TID, and had his stump JP drain removed January 12. He was discharged on cefdinir and gabapentin for phantom and neuropathic pain.

By February 12, 2024, phantom limb pain rated 8/10 and severe stump hypersensitivity prompted an increase in gabapentin to 600mg TID and referral for desensitization therapy. At five-month follow-up on June 18, 2024, Dr. Vance identified a 1.5 cm tender nodule reproducing electric shock sensations — a post-amputation neuroma of the ulnar/median nerves that had failed conservative management. On November 12, 2024, Vance excised a 1.8 x 1.4 cm neuroma and transposed the proximal median and ulnar nerve stumps into the triceps muscle with 5-0 epineural sutures.

Prosthetic fitting followed: a custom myoelectric transhumeral prosthesis was delivered and calibrated on February 5, 2025, by Robert Chen, CPO, with electrode training beginning February 10 and progressive PT through grasping drills, bilateral coordination tasks, and fine motor control training into 2026, despite scattered no-shows in May and November 2025. By June 22, 2026, Sarah Jenkins, PT, DPT, discharged him from comprehensive rehabilitation with near-normal right shoulder range of motion, cleared to return to modified light/medium duty at his employer.
